Cheshunt.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Lee Valley
s1loc: Cheshunt sits at the heart of the Lee Valley Regional Park, and its marquee draw is Paradise Wildlife Park, the only zoo in Britain to hold all five big cats alongside its dinosaur trail and miniature railway. The Lee Valley White Water Centre, a 2012 Olympic legacy venue at Waltham Cross, brings rafting and paddlesport crowds to the River Lee corridor through the season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the water and the green chain, led by the 1,000-acre River Lee Country Park with its flooded gravel pits, wader scrapes and surfaced cycling trails. Cheshunt Park offers gardens, a lake and a skate park, while the towpath, angling lakes and the marinas at Cheshunt and nearby Waltham Abbey keep the warmer-weather visitor flow steady.

Heritage and culture in the area reach back to Theobalds Park and the old royal estate where King James I kept a palace, with Waltham Abbey Gardens and the Royal Gunpowder Mills a short hop south. The Lowewood Museum at neighbouring Hoddesdon and the broad Lee Valley events calendar of open-air activity days give operators a year-round programme along the corridor.

The visitor trade leans on a roadside hotel base around the A10 and Travelodge Cheshunt, plus a guide and activity-operator scene built around the country park and the white water centre. Cheshunt railway station on the West Anglia line and the M25 junctions at nearby Enfield put central London and Hertford within an easy day trip, feeding a constant commuter-belt and seasonal draw.

Wellingborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Nene Valley
s1loc: Wellingborough anchors a Nene Valley visitor economy built on water and heritage, with the Chester House Estate just off the A45 opening a Roman and medieval site to the public alongside its archaeology store and event barns. The market town on the River Nene traces back to a 6th-century Anglo-Saxon settlement, and the All Saints and All Hallows churches give the old centre real depth for visitors.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the valley lakes, led by Stanwick Lakes, a 750-acre nature reserve and adventure attraction with two major play grounds, a zip wire, cycle hire and an open-air theatre. Summer Leys nature reserve draws birdwatchers to its bird hides, and Sywell Country Park, set around an Edwardian reservoir, adds a butterfly garden and waterside walks for families through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Castle Theatre, the area's premier performing-arts venue opened in 1995 on the old cattle-market site beside Wellingborough Museum. The Nene Court shopping village, set in former Victorian shoe-factory buildings on the Embankment, hosts regular artisan markets, independent traders and a microbrewery, carrying the town's long footwear-trade past into a lively independent shopping and events scene along the river.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the country parks and the Nene. Rushden Lakes nearby blends big-name retail with boardwalk cafes and the Nene Wetlands on the doorstep, and Wellingborough railway station on the Midland Main Line runs direct to London St Pancras, feeding a steady day-trip flow from Kettering and Northampton.

Kingston upon Thames.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of riverside south west London
s1loc: Kingston upon Thames runs a busy riverside visitor economy about 12 miles from central London, with the ancient market town set along the Thames and the Coronation Stone of the Saxon kings at its civic heart. Hampton Court Palace, the former home of Henry VIII with its Tudor courts and great gardens, sits a short boat ride or cycle upstream and anchors the area's marquee draw.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into the royal parks, led by Bushy Park with its red and fallow deer, the Diana Fountain and the Chestnut Avenue, and Richmond Park a short ride away with King Henry's Mound. The Thames itself carries rowing, paddleboarding and river-cruise trips from the Kingston piers, while the riverside paths draw walkers and cyclists across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the Rose Theatre, built in the spirit of the Elizabethan original, and Kingston Museum, which tells the town's story and the work of motion-photography pioneer Eadweard Muybridge. The medieval Clattern Bridge, the All Saints church and the Ancient Market Place give the centre its character, with a year-round events calendar along the riverside.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base across the town and a guide scene built around the palace and the river, with Hampton Court and Kingston stations carrying South Western trains in from Waterloo. The draw of Twickenham and its rugby fixtures, the Thames towpath and the parks feeds a strong day-trip and seasonal flow from across the capital and the wider south east.

Andover.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Test Valley
s1loc: Andover sits at the head of the Test Valley in north west Hampshire, and its marquee draw is the Hawk Conservancy Trust, an award-winning attraction set in 22 acres of woodland and wildflower meadow with around 150 birds of prey and daily flying displays. The Iron Age hill fort at Danebury, one of the most studied sites of its kind in Britain, lies just to the south west and frames the town's deep prehistoric past.

The leisure and activity layer runs through the chalk-stream countryside, with the 44-mile Test Way long-distance path and the rose gardens at National Trust Mottisfont within easy reach. Walking, fishing and cycling fill the valley, while Whitchurch Silk Mill nearby keeps its working Victorian machinery turning and the surrounding downland draws families across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on Andover Museum, housed in a Georgian town house of the 1750s, and the adjoining Museum of the Iron Age, which tells the Danebury story. The Lights is the town's professional arts and entertainment venue and the creative hub for north west Hampshire, carrying touring theatre, music and comedy through a year-round programme.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the conservancy and the valley walks. Andover railway station on the West of England line links Waterloo, Salisbury and the south west, and the A303 corridor towards Stonehenge puts the town within an easy day trip of Winchester and the wider Wessex draw, feeding a steady seasonal flow.

Llanelli.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Carmarthen Bay
s1loc: Llanelli built its visitor economy along the Burry Inlet and Carmarthen Bay, led by the 500-acre WWT Llanelli Wetland Centre, home to Caribbean flamingos and tens of thousands of wintering birds. The Millennium Coastal Park stretches some 13 miles of flat, family-friendly path and cycleway along the shore, with its Discovery Centre and the North Dock marina anchoring the seafront draw.

The leisure and activity layer reaches out to Pembrey Country Park, with its eight-mile Blue Flag beach, dry ski slope, toboggan run and adventure play, and the Machynys Peninsula links championship golf course on the coast. Watersports, cycling and the equestrian and nature trails at Pembrey keep operators busy through the warmer season along Carmarthen Bay.

Heritage and culture centre on Parc Howard, the Italianate mansion and gardens housing the Llanelli Museum and its renowned collection of Llanelli pottery. The town's tinplate and rugby past runs deep through the centre, and the mansion grounds, the formal gardens and a busy local events calendar at Parc Howard give Llanelli a year-round cultural pull alongside the draw of the open coast.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base across the town and coast and a guide scene built around the wetlands and the coastal park, with Parc y Scarlets the modern home of the Scarlets and Llanelli RFC drawing fixture and event crowds. Llanelli railway station links Swansea and Cardiff Central, and the heritage Llanelli and Mynydd Mawr Railway adds to a steady day-trip and seasonal flow.

Neath.region: Neath and the Vale of Neath
Neath.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of Neath
s1loc: Neath built its visitor draw on the Vale of Neath and its industrial past, led by the National Trust falls and waterwheel at Aberdulais, where a tidal river once powered tinplate works. The ruined Cistercian Neath Abbey, founded in 1130 and once called the fairest abbey in all of Wales, and the Norman Neath Castle give the old town its marquee heritage anchors.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the Gnoll Estate Country Park, with its trails around ponds, ruins and gushing cascades above the town, and the wider waterfall country of the upper Vale of Neath. The Neath and Tennant canal carries boat trips inland from the town centre from Easter through summer, and the walkable towpath and valley paths keep families and walkers busy across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Cefn Coed Colliery Museum at Crynant in the Dulais Valley, set on what was once the deepest anthracite mine in the world, with its steam winding engine and simulated underground gallery. The Gwyn Hall in the town centre carries concerts, exhibitions and theatre, and Victoria Gardens gives the centre a green heart for the local events calendar.

The visitor trade leans on a town and valley hotel base and a guide scene built around the abbey, the canal and the waterfall walks. Neath railway station on the South Wales Main Line links Swansea, Cardiff and the west, and the M4 corridor puts the coast and the Brecon Beacons fringe within an easy day trip, feeding a steady seasonal flow up the valley.

Bridgend.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Bridgend coast
s1loc: Bridgend county carries a strong coastal visitor economy led by Porthcawl, whose promenade was built in 1887 for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee and whose 1930s Grand Pavilion still anchors the seafront. The Norman ruin of Newcastle Castle, cared for by Cadw, commands the river crossing in the town itself, giving the area both a marquee coast and a hilltop heritage draw.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the shore and inland, with the Blue Flag, lifeguarded Rest Bay a magnet for surfing and its watersports centre, and Coney Beach Pleasure Park bringing the fairground crowds to Porthcawl. Bryngarw Country Park spreads over 100 acres of parkland, and Parc Slip nature reserve offers 300 acres of grassland, woodland and wetland restored from former opencast workings.

Heritage and culture centre on the Merthyr Mawr National Nature Reserve, whose great dunes include the Big Dipper, the highest dune in Wales, set beside historic estate parkland. The Porthcawl Elvis Festival draws over 30,000 fans each autumn, and the woodland Between The Trees festival near Merthyr Mawr adds music, art and natural science to a lively events calendar.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base across Bridgend and Porthcawl and a guide scene built around the coast and the country parks, with the McArthurGlen designer outlet drawing day-trip retail crowds. Bridgend railway station on the South Wales Main Line links Cardiff and Swansea and the M4 puts Barry and the Vale of Glamorgan within easy reach, feeding a strong seasonal flow along the coast.
